1: The door back out to Warrior City.
V: Marble walls, polished until you can see how poor you look in them.
K: Deposit boxes, floor to ceiling. The big ones have names on them: champions. The small ones have numbers.
There are no very small ones.
G: The vault door. Three brass dials, nought to nine.
Engraved round the rim: THE BOOKS BALANCE. READ THEM IN ORDER.
U: The tellers' counter, behind a brass grille. Gold goes in one side. Less gold comes out the other.
t: A writing table. Deposit slips, and a quill on a chain. The chain is stronger than the quill.
i: LEDGER I: RATIONS. By household, by the strength of the child.
CHAMPION'S HOUSEHOLD: FULL MEASURE, AND MEAT ON FEAST DAYS. FIT CHILD: THREE-QUARTERS. MIDDLING CHILD: HALF.
UNFIT CHILD: STRUCK OFF. REMOVED TO THE DESERTERS' CAMP. NO MEASURE.
At the foot of the page, the only line in red ink: HOUSEHOLDS STRUCK OFF THIS MONTH: 6.
j: LEDGER II: STIPENDS. Paid to champions of the Kaloseum on the first of the month. In gold. By hand. With a bow.
MOTHERS OF CHAMPIONS: PAID AS GODDESSES. It has its own column. Then its own page. Then, frankly, its own book.
One line in red ink: CHAMPIONS RETIRED HURT: 2. STIPENDS STOPPED. SEE HOSPITAL.
l: Across the top of the page, in letters a finger high: SPOILS OF THE ISLAND. 500 SOLDIERS. ONE DAY.
Below it, gold, timber, grain and ships, carried forward, and forward, and forward.
One line in red ink: SOLDIERS LOST: 1. (TRIPPED GETTING OFF THE BOAT.)
q: THE WAR CHEST. The great ledger, on a stand of its own, as thick as a door.
Every page says the same thing in bigger numbers. At the bottom of the last one: FOR THE MARCH.
Not a drop of red ink in it anywhere. Whoever keeps this book has never once lost.
_: The bank wall. Thicker than it needs to be. Everything in here is.

objects.name: Master Coyne
lines: Welcome to the Bank of Warrior City. Strength is wealth.
You look... liquid. Moderately.

questions.ask: What does the bank do?
answer: We keep the kingdom's gold. We count it. Then we count it again. It's very relaxing.
And we pay the strong. The king's orders: the stronger the child, the fuller the plate. It's all in the ledgers.
Do have a look. Nobody would dare take one.

questions.ask: Where does all the gold come from?
answer: The island, mostly. Five hundred of ours went over one morning and were back for supper.
We've had to build three new strongrooms since. Spoils are murder on the floors.

questions.ask: Who's the war chest for?
answer: The march, of course. On the wizards. Any day now, His Majesty says.
Wars are expensive. Luckily, so is everything else, and we've been saving.

questions.ask: Must be nice, counting other people's money.
answer: It is, thank you. Better than counting your own, I imagine. Quicker, too.
Mind the step on the way out. It's marble. It's worth more than you.

objects.name: Vaultwarden Grimsby
lines: The vault. Nobody goes in without the combination.
I don't know it. I only guard it. It's safer that way. For me.

questions.ask: Where would I find the combination?
answer: Where everything is, in this building: in the books.
Master Coyne says a banker reads the red ink first. Everyone else reads the totals, and feels good about themselves.

questions.ask: What's in there?
answer: The war chest. All of it.
And one small chest that isn't in any ledger at all. It keeps Master Coyne up at night.

questions.ask: Step aside, or I'll make you.
answer: You'd have to get through me. Then the door. The door's the hard part.
I'm mostly decorative.

objects.name: Clerk Dimmock
lines: Rations. I do the rations. Every household, by the strength of its child.
It's very simple. Strong child: dinner. Weak child: directions.

questions.ask: What happens to the families you strike off?
answer: North, to the deserters' camp. No measure, no stipend, nothing.
I write them in red. Then I never have to write them again.

questions.ask: You sound like you enjoy it.
answer: I don't enjoy anything. That's why they gave me the rations.

objects.name: Clerk Pennywhistle
lines: Stipends! The happy ledger. Champions get gold, by hand, with a bow.
Their mothers get more. Like goddesses, the king says. We had to order a bigger quill.

questions.ask: And when a champion gets hurt?
answer: Then he isn't one. I draw a line through him, in red.
The hospital keeps a ledger too. Theirs is sadder than mine.

questions.ask: A bigger quill. Compensating for something?
answer: ...It's a perfectly normal quill for a person of my responsibilities.

objects.name: Clerk Tallis
lines: Spoils. Mine's the big one. Well. Second biggest. Nobody beats the war chest.

questions.ask: What was the island?
answer: Some nation over the water. The nearest one. Five hundred of ours went over in the morning, and it was ours by supper.
One day. It's written at the top of my page. The king had it written very large.

questions.ask: Anyone lost?
answer: One. Tripped getting off the boat. I've put him in red.
It feels unkind. But the book has to balance.

questions.ask: Stolen goods, then. You're a thief with a pen.
answer: Spoils, if you please. Stolen goods are what other people take.
Different column entirely.

objects.name: Dame Hulda
lines: Mind the gown, dear. It's the king's gift. So is the house. So is the carriage. So is the other carriage.
I'm a mother of champions. Three of them. Strength runs in the family. Mostly down one side.

questions.ask: What's it like, being a goddess?
answer: Exhausting. The bank sends a man to pay me, and another man to carry it, and another man to carry him.
I'd swap the lot to have my boys home for supper. Don't tell the bank.

questions.ask: Where are your sons now?
answer: Two are champions.
One's in the hospital. They don't pay goddesses for that one.

questions.ask: Nice work. Paid to have children.
answer: It is lovely work. Try it.
Oh, you can't. Shame. Off you go.

objects.name: Champion Rask
lines: Stipend day. Mine comes in gold, by hand, with a bow. I like the bow best.

questions.ask: What do you do for it?
answer: Won the culling games at eighteen. Since then: be strong, live in town, have lots of children.
Good job. The only bad day is the day you're not strong any more. Nobody's said what happens then.

questions.ask: Can you count it, or does the bow do that?
answer: ...One. Two. Bow.
It's always the right amount. They'd never cheat a champion.

objects.name: Lord Ferrant
lines: A deposit. A large one. Don't stare. It isn't polite and it isn't yours.

questions.ask: How did you get so rich?
answer: My grandson can lift a cart. Before him we lived by the north gate, eating soup made of the idea of soup.
Now I've a house by the Kaloseum and an account here. Strength is wealth, the sign says. Mine is technically his.

questions.ask: So you've never done a day's work.
answer: I've done a great many days of being related.
It's harder than it looks. Feast days are a nightmare.

objects.name: Old Agna
lines: I'm here to ask for a loan. I've been asking since the spring.
They say come back when my grandson's stronger. He's nine. He's trying.

questions.ask: What if he isn't strong enough?
answer: Then at twelve they'll take him to the Yard, and look at him, and we'll go north to the camp.
I've packed already. You pack early in this city. Saves time.

questions.ask: I hope he grows strong.
answer: So do I, dear. So does the bank. It's the only thing we agree on.

questions.ask: Have you tried being richer?
answer: Do you know, I hadn't. I'll go home and try it now.

objects.name: Bank Guard
lines: No running. No shouting. No punching.
This is the one building in the city where you can't. It's very hard on me.
A board on a stand: TODAY'S RATES.
CHAMPIONS: WE PAY YOU. MOTHERS OF CHAMPIONS: WE PAY YOU MORE.
EVERYONE ELSE: YOU PAY US. FORTY IN THE HUNDRED, MONTHLY.
Underneath, smaller: STRENGTH IS WEALTH.
